tip: Possessives match the noun owned, not the owner. окно (okno = window) is neuter, so моё (moyo = my), not мой (moy) or моя (moya).
его (yego = his) never changes form. Whatever the noun's gender or case, it stays его: его работа (rabota = work).
чей (chey = whose) agrees with the owned thing. зонт (zont = umbrella) is masculine, so чей; a feminine noun takes чья (chya).
свою (svoyu = his own) points back to the subject: любит свою работу (lyubit svoyu rabotu = loves his own job); его (yego) could mean someone else's.
нравится (nravitsya = is pleasing) puts the liker in the dative: Моим родителям (moim roditelyam = my parents). The thing liked is the grammatical subject.
гордиться (gorditsya = to be proud) takes the instrumental with no preposition: гордимся своим городом (gordimsya svoim gorodom = we're proud of our city).
скучать (skuchat = to miss) uses по (po) plus the dative: скучаем по своему дому (skuchaem po svoyemu domu = we miss our home).
ни ... ни (ni ... ni = neither ... nor) still needs a negated verb: ни он, ни она не знали (ni on, ni ona ne znali = neither he nor she knew).
а (a) joins clauses with a light contrast, softer than 'but': звонил, а никто не ответил (zvonil, a nikto ne otvetil = called, but nobody answered).
который (kotoryy = which) takes its gender from the noun it replaces but its case from its own clause: в котором (v kotorom) is prepositional, matching дом (dom = house).
чей (chey) also serves as relative 'whose', agreeing with the owned noun: Собака, чей хозяин ушёл (sobaka, chey khozyain ushyol = the dog whose owner left).
For places, где (gde = where) can replace в котором (v kotorom): Город, где я родился (gorod, gde ya rodilsya = the city where I was born).
After кто (kto = who) the verb stays singular even for many people: тех, кто помог (tekh, kto pomog = those who helped), not помогли (pomogli).
то, что (to, chto = what) joins a main clause to a relative one: то (to) sits first, что (chto) opens the second, as in то, что мне нужно (mne nuzhno = I need).
When the subject stays the same, чтобы (chtoby) takes an infinitive: позвонил, чтобы узнать (pozvonil, chtoby uznat = called to find out).
With a different subject, чтобы (chtoby) needs a past-form verb, not an infinitive: сказал, чтобы мы открыли (skazal, chtoby my otkryli = told us to open).
Russian uses the future in both halves of a real future condition: поедем, если будет (poyedem, yesli budet = we'll go if it is), where English keeps the present.
словно (slovno = as if) introduces an unreal comparison: говорила так, словно знала всё (govorila tak, slovno znala vsyo = spoke as if she knew everything).
Times of day take the instrumental, no preposition: Утром (utrom = in the morning), from утро (utro). Likewise вечером (vecherom), днём (dnyom), ночью (nochyu).
по (po) plus the dative plural means 'every' or 'on': По вечерам (po vecheram = in the evenings) marks a regular, repeated action.
с собой (s soboy = with oneself) is the reflexive 'with him/her': носит с собой (nosit s soboy = carries with him).
вместо того чтобы (vmesto togo chtoby = instead of) is followed by an infinitive, here отдыхать (otdykhat = to rest).
Мало того что (malo togo chto = not only that) sets up an added point, often paired with ещё и (yeshchyo i = and also).
либо ... либо (libo ... libo = either ... or) is the paired 'either/or', a touch more formal than или (ili).
